backlog.spec: Inside fit_predict, before fitting the final SVR, choose the regularization constant C by an inner 5-fold cross-validation on the training set only. Compute the train-train min/max Tanimoto kernel once, then for each C in [1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0] run a 5-fold KFold(shuffle=True, random_state=seed) over the kernel rows and columns (slicing the precomputed kernel, never recomputing it), scoring each fold by Spearman correlation of the held-out predictions against the standardized rank target. Pick the C with the best mean Spearman, refit the SVR on the full training kernel with that C, and use it in the blend exactly as now. Keep epsilon at 0.1. This is cheap because the kernel is reused, and C has never been tuned since it was set to 5.0 by hand.
backlog.title: Pick the SVR C by a small inner CV

backlog.spec: Change the SVR C from 5.0 to 2.0 for stronger regularization on the min/max Tanimoto kernel. Keep other settings the same.
backlog.title: Lower SVR C to 2 with epsilon 0.1

backlog.spec: Compute MACCS keys (rdkit.Chem.MACCSkeys.GenMACCSKeys) for all molecules as 167-bit vectors. Build a min/max count-style Tanimoto kernel on these bits, reusing the existing tanimoto() helper. Train a second precomputed SVR (C=5.0, epsilon=0.1) on the same rank-standardized target and add its rank-normalized test prediction to the blend with equal weight alongside the existing RF/XGB and Morgan SVR members. Do not change the Morgan kernel.
backlog.title: MACCS-keys Tanimoto kernel for a second SVR

backlog.spec: Add a third blend member: a LightGBM regressor with boosting_type='dart', averaged over 3 seeds. Reuse the existing xgb_features matrices (compute them once and pass them to both the XGBoost and the LightGBM, so the expensive featurization is not repeated). Use roughly n_estimators=600, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=15, feature_fraction=0.3, bagging_fraction=0.7, bagging_freq=1, min_child_samples=10, drop_rate=0.1, n_jobs=8, verbose=-1, with random_state=seed+i for i in 0..2, fitted on the same rank target. Rank-normalize the mean of the three predictions and return the equally weighted sum of the three rank vectors (XGB, SVR, dart LGBM). Dart's dropout makes its errors less correlated with plain gradient boosting than the CatBoost/RF/LightGBM-gbdt third members already tried.
backlog.title: Add a seed-bagged dart LightGBM as a third member

backlog.spec: In fit_predict, replace the min/max Tanimoto kernel used by the precomputed SVR with a Laplacian kernel K(a,b) = exp(-gamma * L1(a,b)) on the same 2048-bit radius-2 count vectors, where gamma = 1 / (mean pairwise L1 distance over the training set). Build the training and test kernel matrices with scipy.spatial.distance.cdist(metric='cityblock'). Keep C=5.0, epsilon=0.1, and the rank-normalized standardized target unchanged. The XGBoost branch and the rank-sum blend stay as they are.
backlog.title: Laplacian kernel on Morgan count vectors for SVR

backlog.spec: Make no change to train.py at all; submit the current file as-is so the harness runs it a second time. The incumbent score of 0.4718 comes from a single run, and the per-job noise sd is about 0.0070, so the true loss could plausibly be anywhere in roughly 0.458-0.486. Several recent candidates (CatBoost third member 0.4678, FCFP4 kernel 0.4637/0.4771, ECFP6 kernel 0.4658, averaged Avalon kernel 0.4683) scored below the incumbent but were rejected as within noise; whether they are real improvements depends on where the incumbent actually sits. A second independent run of the incumbent halves the uncertainty on the reference point and makes every future accept/reject decision sharper. No code edit is needed, only a re-run.
backlog.title: Replicate the incumbent unchanged

backlog.spec: Fit 5 SVRs, each on a random 80% subsample of the training rows. Draw the subsamples with np.random.default_rng(seed). Slice the precomputed train kernel for each one, and average the test predictions before ranking. Compute the kernels once.
backlog.title: Seed-bagged SVR on subsamples

backlog.spec: Because every fold tests on unseen Murcko scaffolds, training molecules from large scaffold families are effectively redundant and dominate the tree model's fit. Compute the Bemis-Murcko scaffold SMILES of each training molecule with rdkit.Chem.Scaffolds.MurckoScaffold.MurckoScaffoldSmiles, count how many training molecules share each scaffold, and pass sample_weight = 1/count (or 1/sqrt(count) if that is simpler to justify; pick 1/count) to the XGBoost fit, normalized so the weights average 1. Leave the SVR branch, the features, the target transform and the blend untouched. This makes the tree model's effective training distribution closer to the scaffold-balanced test distribution.
backlog.title: Scaffold-frequency sample weights for the tree model

backlog.spec: Sharpen the SVR's similarity measure by exponentiating the min/max Tanimoto kernel elementwise: after computing K = tanimoto(A, B), use K**3 (and the same transform for both the train-train and test-train matrices) as the precomputed kernel. A raw min/max kernel over count fingerprints is fairly flat -- most pairs sit in a narrow mid-similarity band -- so cubing it increases the contrast between genuine near-neighbours and the bulk, which is what matters when a fold tests on unseen scaffolds. Elementwise powers of a Tanimoto kernel remain positive semidefinite, so no regularization hack is needed. Keep C=5.0 and epsilon=0.1 and the rest of the pipeline identical; implement it as a one-line change inside or just after tanimoto().
backlog.title: Power-transform the Tanimoto kernel

backlog.spec: Swap the epsilon-SVR for sklearn.svm.NuSVR with kernel='precomputed', nu=0.5, C=5.0, on exactly the same min/max Tanimoto kernel and the same standardized rank target, keeping the blend unchanged. With a rank target the residual scale is fixed and known, so the fraction-of-support-vectors parameterization of nu-SVR is a more natural fit than a hand-set epsilon tube of 0.1 in rank-sd units; nu directly controls how much of the training set contributes. If NuSVR is noticeably slower, cap it with max_iter left at default and nothing else; the kernel is only 970x970 so runtime is not a concern.
backlog.title: Use nu-SVR instead of epsilon-SVR

backlog.spec: Keep the min/max Tanimoto similarity computation in tanimoto() but pass the result through an exponential before the SVR sees it: in fit_predict, wrap both kernel matrices as np.exp(-GAMMA*(1.0 - K)) with GAMMA = 3.0, where K is the raw min/max similarity. Add GAMMA as a module-level setting. The raw Tanimoto kernel is close to linear in similarity, so a molecule at similarity 0.3 still exerts meaningful pull on the prediction; the exponential form compresses the influence of distant molecules and emphasizes close structural neighbors, which is the regime where measured hepatocyte clearance actually transfers. This is the standard way to turn a similarity into a Laplacian-style kernel and keeps the matrix positive semi-definite in practice. A related exp(-2*(1-T)) kernel was tried in slot 33, but only as an extra third blend member on Avalon features, never as a replacement for the existing Morgan-count kernel of the current SVR.
backlog.title: Sharpen the Tanimoto kernel with an exponential transform

backlog.spec: Add scaffold-frequency sample weights to the XGBoost fit. Import MurckoScaffold from rdkit.Chem.Scaffolds, compute the Murcko scaffold SMILES for every training molecule, count how many training molecules share each scaffold, and build weights w_i = 1/sqrt(count of molecule i's scaffold), normalized to mean 1. Pass these as sample_weight to model.fit. Because the harness keeps a whole scaffold inside one fold, each test fold is made of skeletons the model has never seen, so what matters is learning structure-transferable signal rather than fitting the few over-represented scaffold families well. Down-weighting large scaffold clusters stops a handful of congeneric series from dominating the loss surface and should push the trees toward splits that generalize across skeletons. Leave the SVR branch, the rank target and the blend untouched so the effect is attributable to the weights alone.
backlog.title: Weight training molecules by inverse scaffold frequency

backlog.spec: Replace the XGBRegressor in the XGBoost branch with xgboost.XGBRanker using objective='rank:pairwise', all training molecules in a single query group, and the same tree settings (max_depth 4, 600 trees, lr 0.03, subsample 0.7, colsample 0.3, min_child_weight 3, reg_lambda 5). Feed it the rank-normalized target as relevance labels cast to integers in 0..20 (multiply by 20 and round). Predictions are used only for rank-blending, so the scale does not matter. The SVR branch and blend stay the same.
backlog.title: XGBoost with pairwise ranking objective

backlog.spec: Inside fit_predict, compute out-of-fold SVR predictions on the training set with an inner 5-fold KFold (shuffle, random_state=seed) using the existing precomputed Tanimoto SVR. Fit the XGBoost model on descriptor plus fingerprint features to the residual target (rank target minus the out-of-fold SVR prediction), instead of the rank target. For test molecules, add the SVR prediction fitted on all training data to the XGBoost residual prediction. Blend the resulting prediction with the plain SVR prediction by rank average, equal weights.
backlog.title: Residual XGBoost on out-of-fold SVR predictions

backlog.spec: In tanimoto(), return the kernel raised to the power 2 (num**2) before it is passed to the SVR. It stays positive semidefinite, and it sharpens similarity toward near neighbours. Apply it to both train-train and test-train kernels.
backlog.title: Power-transformed Tanimoto kernel

backlog.spec: Replace the single precomputed SVR fit with an average over three bootstrap replicates. Compute the full kernels Ktr = tanimoto(Xtr, Xtr) and Kte = tanimoto(Xte, Xtr) once, as now. Then for b in range(3), draw a bootstrap sample of row indices idx with a numpy Generator seeded by seed+b, fit SVR(kernel='precomputed', C=5.0, epsilon=0.1) on Ktr[np.ix_(idx, idx)] with the correspondingly indexed standardized target, predict on Kte[:, idx], rank-normalize that prediction, and accumulate. Use the mean of the three rank vectors as p_svr in the final blend. Bagging a kernel method reduces the variance that comes from individual support vectors in a small 970-molecule dataset, and the kernel slices are cheap because the expensive min/max computation is done only once. Three replicates keep the runtime well inside the 10-minute budget.
backlog.title: Average three SVR fits over bootstrap resamples of the training set

backlog.spec: Add test-time augmentation at the featurization level. Write a helper that, given a SMILES string and a seed, returns a list of K=5 equivalent SMILES by calling Chem.MolToSmiles(mol, doRandom=True, canonical=False) with the RDKit random seed set deterministically from the harness seed, always including the canonical form as one of the K. In fit_predict, build the XGBoost test matrix by featurizing all K variants of every test molecule, predicting each, and averaging the K predictions per molecule before rank-normalizing. Train on canonical SMILES only. Most descriptors and all fingerprints are graph-canonical and so invariant to SMILES writing order, which means the averaging is a no-op for them; the point is to catch and smooth any order-dependent descriptor columns in Descriptors.descList and to verify empirically that the feature pipeline is genuinely invariant. If the loss is unchanged within noise, that is itself a useful negative result that rules out a whole class of worry. Keep the SVR branch and the blend unchanged.
backlog.title: Average each molecule's prediction over its own randomized SMILES

backlog.spec: Build 10 precomputed SVRs. Each one uses a random 50 percent of the 2048 Morgan count bits, selected with np.random.default_rng(seed + k) for k in 0..9, and its own min/max Tanimoto kernel computed on that column subset. Each SVR uses C=5.0, epsilon=0.1 and the rank-standardized target. Average the 10 test predictions (rank-normalized) and use the result in place of the single SVR in the blend, keeping the XGBoost branch and the equal-weight rank blend unchanged.
backlog.title: Random-subspace SVR ensemble over fingerprint bit subsets

backlog.spec: Replace the single XGBoost fit with an average over three fits that each see a random two-thirds of the feature columns. Compute Xtr_f = xgb_features(train_smiles) and Xte_f = xgb_features(test_smiles) once at the top of fit_predict (the current code calls xgb_features three times, which is wasteful and should be fixed anyway). Then for b in range(3), use a numpy Generator seeded by seed+b to choose a random subset of two-thirds of the column indices, fit the existing XGBRegressor configuration with random_state=seed+b on Xtr_f[:, cols], predict Xte_f[:, cols], rank-normalize, and average the three rank vectors into p_rf. The feature matrix mixes descriptors, Morgan counts, Avalon counts and ErG into several thousand columns of very different character, and column bagging decorrelates the members more than reseeding alone does (a plain 5-seed average scored 0.4722, i.e. no gain). Caching the features offsets most of the added cost.
backlog.title: Average predictions over bagged XGBoost feature subsets

backlog.spec: The final line of fit_predict currently returns rankdata(p_rf)/len(p_rf) + rankdata(p_svr)/len(p_svr), an exactly equal blend. Change it to a weighted blend favoring the SVR: 0.6*rankdata(p_svr)/len(p_svr) + 0.4*rankdata(p_rf)/len(p_rf). The two members have never had their relative weight varied, and there is reason to think the SVR deserves more: the Tanimoto min/max kernel generalizes across unseen Murcko scaffolds by direct structural similarity, which is exactly what the scaffold-grouped folds test, whereas the tree model keys on descriptor thresholds learned from the scaffolds present in training. Since Spearman only cares about ordering, the weighting acts purely on the relative influence of the two rank vectors. Keep both members and all their hyperparameters unchanged; only the two coefficients in the return statement change.
backlog.title: Shift the blend weight toward the SVR (0.6/0.4)

memo: Helped: rank-normalized blending of diverse families (RF+Tanimoto SVR 0.5407 from ~0.6103 baseline); shallow XGBoost on descriptors plus Morgan (0.5195); rank-transformed target (0.4994); Avalon count and ErG fingerprints in XGB features (0.4718, incumbent, one run only, so noisy). Did not help or within the ~0.0070 noise: kNN (0.5427), chiral radius-3 counts (0.5372), ExtraTrees, KernelRidge, Huber LightGBM, Ridge, MLP (0.5029), MACCS (0.4958), column pruning (0.4778), CatBoost as replacement (0.4779, 0.4831) or third member (0.4678), RF swaps (0.4874), 5-seed XGB (0.4722), feature selection (0.4738), Gaussian-rank target (0.4790), XGB retuning (0.4788, 0.4773). Model swaps, extra fingerprints and XGB tuning look exhausted. Kernel variants are near noise: FCFP4 kernel (0.4637/0.4771 over two runs), ECFP6 kernel (0.4658). Next: replicate the incumbent 0.4718, tune SVR C/epsilon and blend weights, and try CatBoost as third member together with the FCFP4 kernel. Avoid repeating tried ideas.
